newsitem.title: CHINA: China premier says state firms' reform essential.
newsitem.headline: China premier says state firms' reform essential.

text.p: In an annual report noteworthy for its caution, Chinese Premier Li Peng sounded one bold note on Saturday by placing the thorny issue of reform of loss-making state firms at the heart of his 1997 agenda.

After a year in which the state firms that Beijing calls a pillar of the economy suffered soaring losses and reported their first net loss for a single quarter, Li vowed to tackle reform of the Stalinist-era dinosaurs.

He promised easier loans for better-performing firms and more autonomy in decision-making, urged more sell-offs of stock to employees and stressed the need to use the near-taboo method of bankruptcy to eliminate hopeless cases.

In his government report to the National People's Congress, or parliament, Li said reform to force state enterprises to swim -- or sink -- was so crucial that without it China's socialist system could crumble.

"Development and reform of state enterprises is a major economic problem that relates to the nation's economic development and is also a major political problem which is of vital importance for the destiny of the socialist system."

Li was quoting President Jiang Zemin, successor to paramount leader Deng Xiaoping who died last week at 92. Under Deng's rule China tried to remove the cushion of state subsidies from tens of thousands of state enterprises.

Finance Minister Liu Zhongli, in his budget on Sunday, is to set subsidies for loss-making enterprises at 7.754 billion yuan ($934 million) in 1997 compared with 6.65 billion yuan for 1996 and up by 8.6 percent from the actual amount in 1996.

China has for years tiptoed around the fringes of how to force state firms to compete in the market place, unwilling to confront a shift away from the socialist tenet of public ownership while raising the spectre of unemployment and possible social unrest.
For the first time in years, Li placed policies to force state firms to show a profit -- or go under -- ahead of inflation.
To improve the state sector, the government would focus on rejuvenating large enterprises while giving small ones more freedom, Li said.
More than 60 percent of state revenue derived from state enterprises and two-thirds of all workers in cities and towns worked in state firms, Li said.
About 75 percent of China's biggest 100,000 state firms operate in the red, and the sector reported its first ever net loss in the first quarter of last year.
State firms have since recovered slightly, but officials say they remain a major burden on the economy with losses skyrocketing 45 percent in the first nine months of 1996.

To nurture state firms that do make a profit, Li pledged to expand to 511 from 300 the number of big firms that received priority for loans, and to increase the cities chosen as pilots for implementing bankruptcies and mergers to 110 from 58.

On the sensitive issue of bankruptcy in a system that for years guaranteed cradle-to-grave state care, Li vowed to boost capital reserves in some cities to clear bad debts of merged or bankrupt enterprises.
"Bankrupt enterprises shall be closed and no enterprises shall be allowed to evade payment of debts through declaring bankruptcy," he said.
Bankruptcies in China soared by more than 160 percent last year, to exceed the total for the previous seven years.
Revival of China's estimated 240,000 smaller state enterprises should be pioneered through mergers, joint stock partnerships, leasing and sell-offs, he said.
